lessons.title: Lesson 1: Introduction to Irrigation Systems in African Agriculture
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 4 of the Agricultural Irrigation Technician training. This lesson sets the foundation for everything that follows. Irrigation is not just about water; it is about turning water into income, food security, and resilience. Across Africa, rainfall is increasingly unpredictable. A farmer in Kenya's Makueni County may receive 400 mm of rain in a good year and less than 150 mm in a bad one. A market gardener in Ghana's Greater Accra Region may face a dry spell exactly when tomato seedlings need moisture most. Irrigation bridges that gap. As a technician, your job is to design, install, maintain, and troubleshoot systems that deliver the right amount of water to the right place at the right time, at a cost the farmer can afford. We begin with the big picture. Africa has about 60 percent of the world's uncultivated arable land, yet only about 6 percent of cultivated land is irrigated. That means huge potential. But potential does not pay bills. Farmers need systems that work reliably with local water sources, local energy, and local budgets. There are four main irrigation categories you will encounter. First, surface irrigation, including furrow and basin systems. These are common in rice paddies in Madagascar and along the Nile in Egypt and Sudan. They are cheap to build but can waste water and cause waterlogging. Second, sprinkler irrigation, where water is sprayed through the air like rainfall. This suits cereals, pasture, and vegetables on sandy or sloping soils. Third, drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to the root zone through emitters. Drip is the most water-efficient method and is transforming horticulture in Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, and South Africa. Fourth, sub-surface irrigation, where water is applied below the soil surface, often through buried drip lines. This reduces evaporation and is excellent for high-value crops. Your role as a technician is to match the system to the farm. Consider water source: borehole, river, dam, pond, or municipal supply. Consider energy: diesel pump, electric pump, solar pump, or gravity. Consider crop: maize needs different scheduling than kale or mango. Consider soil: sandy soils drain fast and need frequent small applications; clay soils hold water and need slower, less frequent applications. Consider labour: who will operate the system daily? Consider market: a farmer selling export vegetables can afford drip; a subsistence farmer may start with a treadle pump and furrows. Practical Africa-focused design means using locally available materials where possible. In many countries, PVC and HDPE pipes are available in capital cities but expensive in rural areas. Solar panels have become cheaper and more reliable, but batteries and controllers still fail. Drip tape is affordable but clogs if water is not filtered. Your training will teach you to calculate flow rates, pressure losses, and irrigation schedules. You will learn to read a farmer's field like a doctor reads a patient. You will learn to install a system that a farmer can repair with basic tools. You will learn to train the farmer and farm workers so the system survives after you leave. Business-first thinking is essential. An irrigation system is an investment. A smallholder may spend 200 to 2,000 US dollars on a pump and pipes. That money must return through higher yields, off-season production, or better prices. A technician who ignores economics will install systems that are abandoned within a year. So ask: What is the expected yield increase? What is the cost of water and energy per season? What is the payback period? Can the farmer access credit, subsidy, or a lease arrangement? Finally, remember safety and sustainability. Never oversize a pump that drains a borehole dry. Never install a system that causes soil salinity. Never ignore the needs of women and youth who often do the watering. This module will give you the technical skills, but your success will be measured by the farms that thrive because of your work. In the next lesson, we will dive into water sources and pump selection, where you will learn to measure flow, calculate head, and choose the right pump for African conditions.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Water Sources, Pump Selection, and Solar Solutions
lessons.body: In this lesson, we focus on the heart of any irrigation system: the water source and the pump that moves water from source to field. Without a reliable water source, even the best-designed pipes and emitters are useless. We will cover how to assess water availability, how to measure flow and pressure, how to select pumps, and how to integrate solar power, which is rapidly changing irrigation across Africa. Start with the water source. Common sources include boreholes, shallow wells, rivers, streams, dams, ponds, and municipal or canal supplies. Each has advantages and risks. Boreholes can provide year-round water but may be expensive to drill and may yield less than expected. Shallow wells are cheaper but can dry up in the dry season. Rivers and streams are free but may be seasonal and may require permits. Dams and ponds store water but lose it to evaporation and seepage. Municipal supplies are convenient but often unreliable and costly for agriculture. Your first task is to measure available water. Use a simple bucket and stopwatch method for small sources: fill a known volume and time it. For boreholes, conduct a pump test: pump at a steady rate and record the water level drop over several hours. Calculate the safe yield, which is the maximum rate you can pump without drying the source. A borehole that yields 1,000 litres per hour can support about 0.2 hectares of drip-irrigated vegetables, but only if you schedule properly. Next, understand head and pressure. Head is the height water must be lifted plus friction losses in pipes. Total head equals static lift plus friction loss plus pressure required at the emitters. For example, if a pump lifts water 10 metres from a well, pushes it through 100 metres of pipe with 3 metres of friction loss, and the drip system needs 1 bar (about 10 metres of head), total head is 10 plus 3 plus 10, equal to 23 metres. Flow rate is the volume per unit time, usually litres per hour or cubic metres per hour. You need both head and flow to select a pump. Pump types include centrifugal, submersible, helical rotor, and diaphragm. Centrifugal pumps are common for surface water and are relatively cheap but lose prime if air enters. Submersible pumps sit inside boreholes and push water up; they are efficient but require clean water and electricity or a generator. Helical rotor pumps are positive displacement pumps that work well with solar power and can handle dirty water. Diaphragm pumps are good for low-flow, high-head situations and can run on solar. Solar pumping is a game-changer in Africa. A typical solar pump system includes solar panels, a controller or inverter, a pump, and sometimes a battery or storage tank. The advantage is zero fuel cost and low maintenance. The disadvantage is that pumping depends on sunshine, so you need water storage or a backup. When sizing a solar pump, calculate daily water requirement first. For example, 0.5 hectares of drip-irrigated tomatoes may need 20,000 litres per day. If the pump runs 6 effective sun hours, it must deliver about 3,300 litres per hour. Then match that flow to the head. Solar panels are rated in watts; a rule of thumb is that 1,000 watts of panels can pump about 1,000 litres per hour to 10 metres head, but actual performance varies. Always use manufacturer curves and local solar radiation data. Practical tips for African conditions: use stainless steel or plastic pumps where possible to resist corrosion. Protect panels from theft with locks, fences, or community arrangements. Use a float switch or dry-run protection to avoid burning the pump when the source is empty. Install a sand filter or settling tank before the pump if water is dirty. Keep spare seals, impellers, and controllers on hand because supply chains can be slow. Consider hybrid systems: solar with a diesel or electric backup for cloudy days or peak demand. Also consider gravity systems where a tank is elevated on a hill or tower. Gravity saves energy but requires a tall structure and a large tank. A 10-metre elevation gives about 1 bar of pressure, enough for drip but not for sprinklers. Finally, think about water quality. Test for salinity, iron, and sediment. High salinity can damage crops and clog emitters. Iron bacteria can clog drip lines. Sediment wears pumps and blocks filters. Simple tests include electrical conductivity for salinity and a clear bottle test for sediment. If quality is poor, you may need filtration, settling, or a different water source. In the next lesson, we will design the distribution network: pipes, filters, valves, and emitters. Remember, a pump is only as good as the water source and the system it feeds. Measure twice, install once.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Designing Distribution Networks, Filtration, and Emitters
lessons.body: Now that you understand water sources and pumps, we move to the distribution network: the pipes, fittings, filters, valves, and emitters that carry water from the pump to the plant roots. This is where good design saves money and bad design wastes it. A well-designed network delivers uniform pressure and flow to every plant, is easy to operate, and can be repaired with local tools. We will cover pipe sizing, pressure loss, filtration, and emitter selection, with practical examples from African farms. Start with pipe sizing. Water flowing through a pipe loses pressure due to friction. Smaller pipes and higher flows cause more friction loss. Your goal is to keep friction loss low enough that all emitters receive the required pressure. A common mistake is using a pipe that is too small, which starves the far end of the field. Use friction loss tables or simple calculators. For example, a 32 mm polyethylene pipe carrying 2,000 litres per hour loses about 0.5 bar per 100 metres. A 50 mm pipe carrying the same flow loses only about 0.1 bar per 100 metres. The larger pipe costs more but saves energy and improves uniformity. As a rule, keep mainlines and sub-mainlines at least 50 mm for small farms, and 63 mm or 75 mm for larger farms. Lateral lines, which carry water to emitters, are usually 16 mm or 20 mm for drip tape and 20 mm to 32 mm for sprinklers. Lay out the network in a way that minimizes pipe length and elevation differences. A looped network can improve pressure uniformity but is more complex. A branched network is simpler and cheaper. Use valves to divide the field into blocks so you can irrigate one block at a time. This reduces the required pump size and flow rate. For example, a 1-hectare farm might be divided into four blocks of 0.25 hectares each. Irrigate one block at a time with a smaller pump instead of all four at once with a large pump. This saves money on pumps and pipes. Filtration is critical, especially for drip irrigation. Drip emitters have small openings, often 0.5 to 1.0 mm, and clog easily with sand, silt, clay, algae, and chemical precipitates. Use a combination of filters: a settling tank or pond for large particles, a sand filter for fine particles, and a screen or disc filter for final protection. Screen filters are cheap and easy to clean but clog quickly in dirty water. Disc filters are more robust and can be cleaned by opening and rinsing. Sand filters are expensive but handle heavy organic loads. Always install a pressure gauge before and after the filter to monitor clogging. If the pressure difference exceeds 0.5 bar, clean or backwash the filter. Also install a valve to flush the mainline and laterals regularly. Emitter selection depends on crop, soil, and water quality. Drip emitters come in many types: inline drip tape, online drippers, pressure-compensating drippers, and adjustable drippers. Pressure-compensating drippers maintain a constant flow even if pressure varies, which is excellent for long laterals or hilly fields. Non-pressure-compensating drippers are cheaper but require uniform pressure. For sandy soils, use higher flow emitters and shorter irrigation times. For clay soils, use lower flow emitters and longer times to avoid runoff. For vegetables, drip tape with 30 cm emitter spacing is common. For orchards, use two or four online drippers per tree. Sprinklers are another option. They are easier to inspect and can be moved, but they use more water and energy. Sprinkler spacing should match the throw diameter. For example, a sprinkler with a 12-metre throw should be spaced 12 metres apart in a square pattern. Avoid sprinkling in windy conditions, which causes uneven distribution. Also consider micro-sprinklers and mini-sprinklers for orchards and nurseries. They are more efficient than large sprinklers and less clog-prone than drip. Practical Africa-focused tips: use UV-resistant pipes and fittings because sunlight degrades cheap plastics. Bury mainlines where possible to protect them from animals, theft, and traffic. Use quick-connect fittings for easy repair. Label valves and filters so farmers know what to do. Keep a spare parts kit with extra emitters, connectors, and filter screens. Train the farmer to flush the system weekly and clean filters daily if water is dirty. In the next lesson, we will cover irrigation scheduling and water management, where you will learn to calculate how much water to apply and when. Remember, a distribution network is not just hardware; it is a system that must be understood and maintained by the people who use it.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Irrigation Scheduling, Soil Moisture, and Water Management
lessons.body: Irrigation scheduling is the decision of when to irrigate and how much water to apply. It is the most important skill for a technician because it directly affects yield, water use, energy cost, and soil health. Poor scheduling wastes water, leaches nutrients, and can waterlog or dry out crops. Good scheduling maximizes profit and resilience. In this lesson, we will cover soil moisture basics, crop water requirements, scheduling methods, and practical tools for African farmers. Start with soil. Soil is a mixture of minerals, organic matter, air, and water. The amount of water soil can hold depends on texture. Sandy soils hold little water, perhaps 5 to 10 percent by volume. Loamy soils hold 15 to 25 percent. Clay soils hold 30 to 40 percent but may hold it so tightly that plants cannot extract it. The key concept is field capacity, which is the water remaining after excess water drains away. The permanent wilting point is the water level at which plants can no longer extract water and wilt permanently. Plant available water is the difference between field capacity and wilting point. For irrigation, you want to keep soil moisture between field capacity and about 50 percent depletion. If you let soil dry below that, plants suffer. If you overwater, you lose water to deep percolation and may cause waterlogging. Crop water requirement is the amount of water a crop uses through transpiration and evaporation from the soil, called evapotranspiration or ET. ET depends on weather, crop stage, and crop type. A simple way to estimate ET is to use a pan evaporimeter. Place a standard pan in the field, measure water loss over 24 hours, and multiply by a crop coefficient. For example, if pan evaporation is 6 mm per day and the crop coefficient is 0.8, crop water use is 4.8 mm per day. One millimetre of water over one hectare equals 10,000 litres. So 4.8 mm equals 48,000 litres per hectare per day. That is a lot of water, which is why drip irrigation is so valuable. Scheduling methods range from simple to advanced. The simplest is feel and appearance: dig a handful of soil, squeeze it, and judge moisture. This requires training but costs nothing. A more precise method is using a soil moisture meter or tensiometer. Tensiometers measure soil water tension and are affordable and reliable for vegetables and orchards. They need maintenance and calibration but give clear readings. Another method is the water balance method: track rainfall, irrigation, and ET to estimate soil moisture. This works well if you have reliable weather data. Finally, there are automated sensors and controllers, but they are expensive and may not be suitable for smallholders. For African conditions, I recommend a combination of simple tools and observation. Teach farmers to check soil moisture at 15 cm and 30 cm depth. If the soil at 15 cm is dry but at 30 cm is moist, it is time to irrigate lightly. If both are dry, irrigate more. If both are wet, wait. Also teach them to observe plants: leaves may roll or change color when stressed. But do not wait for wilting; that is too late. Irrigation frequency and duration depend on soil, crop, and system. For drip irrigation on sandy soil, you may irrigate daily or every other day with small amounts. On clay soil, you may irrigate every three to five days with larger amounts. For sprinklers, apply water at a rate the soil can absorb. If water starts to run off, stop and wait, then continue. This is called the soak and cycle method. A practical example: a farmer in Uganda grows tomatoes on a loam soil with drip irrigation. Crop water use is 5 mm per day. Drip emitters apply 2 litres per hour per plant, with plants spaced 0.5 m apart in rows 1 m apart. That is 2 plants per square metre, so each square metre receives 4 litres per hour. To apply 5 mm, which is 5 litres per square metre, the system must run for 1.25 hours. So the farmer irrigates for about 1 hour and 15 minutes daily. If the soil is sandy, split this into two shorter runs. If it is clay, irrigate every second day for 2.5 hours. Water management also includes avoiding salinity and waterlogging. Salts accumulate in the root zone when irrigation water is salty and drainage is poor. To manage salinity, apply extra water occasionally to leach salts below the root zone, but only if drainage is good. Otherwise, salts will rise. Waterlogging occurs when the soil is saturated and roots cannot breathe. Avoid overwatering and ensure drainage channels or raised beds. Finally, consider water harvesting and storage. In many parts of Africa, rainwater harvesting from roofs, roads, or runoff can supplement irrigation. A 100 square metre roof can collect 80,000 litres per year in a region with 800 mm rainfall. That is enough to irrigate a small garden. Store water in tanks, ponds, or sand dams. Also consider mulching to reduce evaporation and conserve soil moisture. In the next lesson, we will cover maintenance, troubleshooting, and business skills, where you will learn to keep systems running and turn irrigation into a profitable enterprise.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Maintenance, Troubleshooting, and Business Skills for Irrigation Technicians
lessons.body: The final lesson of Module 4 brings together everything you have learned and adds the practical skills that keep irrigation systems running and profitable. Maintenance and troubleshooting are what separate a good technician from a great one. Business skills are what turn your technical knowledge into a career. We will cover routine maintenance, common problems and solutions, spare parts management, and how to price and market your services. Routine maintenance prevents most breakdowns. Create a maintenance schedule for every system you install. Daily tasks include checking pump operation, cleaning filters, and inspecting for leaks. Weekly tasks include flushing mainlines and laterals, checking emitter flow, and testing pressure gauges. Monthly tasks include cleaning solar panels, checking pump seals, and lubricating moving parts. Seasonal tasks include draining pipes before frost or dry seasons, replacing worn emitters, and testing water quality. Train the farmer or a designated operator to do daily and weekly tasks. Provide a simple checklist in the local language. Common problems and solutions: First, pump not delivering water. Check power supply, fuel, or solar panel connections. Check for airlocks and prime the pump. Check for clogged intake or worn impeller. Second, low pressure. Check for leaks, closed valves, clogged filters, or undersized pipes. Third, uneven water distribution. Check for clogged emitters, pressure differences, or elevation changes. Fourth, clogged emitters. Flush laterals, clean filters, and consider chemical treatment for algae or precipitates. Fifth, pump running but no water. Check for dry source, closed valve, or broken pipe. Sixth, excessive energy consumption. Check for worn pump, incorrect impeller, or system operating at higher pressure than needed. Seventh, algae growth in tanks or pipes. Cover tanks, add shade, or use approved algaecides. Eighth, rodent damage to drip tape. Use traps, keep field clean, or bury tape slightly. Ninth, theft of panels or pumps. Use locks, fences, or community watch. Tenth, salinity buildup. Leach with extra water if drainage is good, or switch to more salt-tolerant crops. Spare parts management is critical. Keep a kit with extra emitters, connectors, filter screens, seals, impellers, and fuses. Source parts locally where possible. Build relationships with suppliers in your region. For solar systems, keep spare controller and pump parts. For diesel systems, keep fuel filters and oil. Teach farmers to store parts in a dry, secure place. Now, business skills. As an irrigation technician, you can work as an employee, a contractor, or an entrepreneur. You can serve smallholder farmers, commercial farms, NGOs, or government projects. To succeed, you need to price your services correctly. Calculate your costs: transport, tools, labour, materials, and overhead. Add a profit margin of 20 to 30 percent. For installation, charge a fixed fee based on system size, or a daily rate plus materials. For maintenance, offer a monthly or seasonal contract. For training, charge per session or per farmer. Marketing is about trust. In rural Africa, word of mouth is powerful. Do good work, and farmers will recommend you. Attend farmer field days, agricultural shows, and cooperative meetings. Partner with input suppliers, seed companies, and extension officers. Use simple flyers or WhatsApp groups to share tips and photos of your work. Keep records of every job: location, farmer name, system type, costs, and results. This helps you quote future jobs and prove your impact. Consider offering additional services: water testing, soil testing, system design, and solar installation. These add value and income. Also consider selling or leasing equipment. Some technicians rent out pumps, pipes, or solar panels. This can be profitable if you manage logistics and maintenance. Finally, think about scaling. You can train other technicians and build a team. You can specialize in high-value crops, solar pumping, or drip systems. You can seek certification from a recognized body, which builds credibility. Remember, your reputation is your most valuable asset. Be honest about what you can and cannot do. If a job is beyond your skills, refer it to a more experienced technician. Never oversell a system that a farmer cannot afford or maintain. In summary, this module has taken you from the basics of irrigation to the practical skills of design, installation, scheduling, and business. You are now equipped to help African farmers produce more food, earn more income, and use water wisely. The need is enormous, and the opportunity is great. Go out, listen to farmers, measure carefully, install well, and maintain what you build. Your work will change lives.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Irrigation System Sizing, Water Quality, and Technician Business Tools

This Practical Reference lesson is the working companion to Module 4. It is designed to be printed, laminated, and carried in the technician's toolkit. It consolidates the numbers, formulas, water-quality thresholds, and pricing logic that an irrigation technician in Africa needs daily to quote, install, troubleshoot, and maintain systems profitably. The emphasis is business-first: every technical figure is paired with a commercial implication so that the technician can move from diagnosis to a paid solution quickly.

1. Core Sizing Formulas Every Technician Must Memorise

System sizing begins with crop water demand. The reference evapotranspiration (ETo) is adjusted by the crop coefficient (Kc) to give crop water use (ETc), and then divided by system efficiency to give the gross irrigation requirement. In African smallholder and commercial settings, efficiency values range from 50â60% for furrow, 65â75% for sprinkler, and 85â95% for drip with proper filtration and pressure regulation.

ETc = ETo Ã Kc
Gross irrigation requirement = ETc Ã· system efficiency
System flow rate (L/h) = (Area in mÂ² Ã Gross application in mm) Ã· (Operating hours Ã 1,000)

For a one-hectare (10,000 mÂ²) tomato plot in a semi-arid zone with ETo of 6 mm/day, Kc of 1.15, and drip efficiency of 90%, the crop demand is 6.9 mm/day, gross demand is 7.7 mm/day, and with 6 operating hours the required flow is approximately 12,800 L/h, or roughly 12.8 mÂ³/h. A technician quoting a pump must add 15â20% headroom for fouling and future expansion.

2. Water Quality Thresholds and Treatment Decisions

Water quality determines whether a drip system survives or fails within one season. The technician must test at source before installation and record results on the quotation. The table below summarises the thresholds most relevant to African surface and borehole sources.

Table 1: Irrigation Water Quality Thresholds and Technician Action
Parameter Safe Range Problem Range Technician Action
pH6.5â8.0<6.0 or >8.5Acid injection or buffering; re-test monthly
Electrical conductivity (ECw)<0.75 dS/m>1.5 dS/mLeaching fraction, salt-tolerant crops, blend source
Total suspended solids<50 mg/L>100 mg/LSand filter + settling tank; screen backup
Iron (Fe)<0.2 mg/L>1.5 mg/LAeration, settling, acid flush; avoid drip without treatment
Manganese (Mn)<0.1 mg/L>1.5 mg/LOxidation + filtration; chlorination shock
Bicarbonate (HCO3)<90 mg/L>200 mg/LAcid injection to prevent calcium carbonate scaling
Faecal coliforms0 CFU/100 mL for vegetables>0 CFU/100 mLStop use for fresh produce; treat or switch source

Sources: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 29 Rev. 1 (Ayers & Westcot, 1985); WHO Guidelines for the Safe Use of Wastewater in Agriculture (2006); University extension guidance on drip system clogging (e.g., UC ANR and Texas A&M AgriLife).

3. Business Pricing and Service Reference

Technicians in Africa often under-price because they quote only materials. A profitable quotation includes labour, transport, commissioning, training, and a maintenance retainer. The table below gives indicative ranges in USD for a 1-hectare drip system, based on regional supplier pricing and technician labour rates. These are reference figures, not fixed prices; the technician must adjust for country, distance, and currency volatility.

Table 2: Indicative Cost and Revenue Structure for a 1 ha Drip Installation

Sources: Compiled from regional supplier catalogues and agribusiness cost studies, including ILRI market analyses and FAO investment cost references for small-scale irrigation in sub-Saharan Africa. Figures are indicative and require local verification.

4. Safety Warning: Waterborne Pathogens and Chemical Handling

â  RED SAFETY WARNING

Irrigation water used on fresh produce can carry Salmonella, E. coli, Vibrio cholerae, and parasitic helminths. Never assume a source is safe because it looks clear. If faecal coliforms are present and the crop is eaten raw, the water is not suitable without treatment. When handling chlorine, acids, or fertiliser injectants, always wear gloves, goggles, and a respirator; never mix acid with chlorine â toxic gas can be released. Store chemicals locked, labelled, and away from children and livestock. Train every worker on first aid and emergency contacts before commissioning the system. Follow WHO Guidelines for the Safe Use of Wastewater in Agriculture and national public health regulations.

5. Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Test water first: pH, EC, iron, manganese, bicarbonate, and faecal coliforms â record on the quotation.
  2. Calculate flow and head: ETc Ã· efficiency, plus 20% headroom, before selecting a pump.
  3. Size filtration to the dirtiest water: sand filter for solids, screen for backup, flush points at every low end.
  4. Pressure-compensate on slopes: use PC emitters where gradient exceeds 2% to avoid dry and flooded zones.
  5. Quote labour, transport, commissioning, and training separately: never bury them in materials.
  6. Offer a maintenance retainer: four visits per year, recurring revenue, written scope.
  7. Train the farmer and one worker: flushing, filter cleaning, valve operation, and emergency shutdown.
  8. Document everything: photos, water test, layout drawing, invoice, and warranty terms signed by both parties.

6. Further Reading

  • FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 â Crop Evapotranspiration (free, full text).
  • FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 29 Rev. 1 â Water Quality for Agriculture (free, full text).
  • WHO Guidelines for the Safe Use of Wastewater, Excreta and Greywater in Agriculture (free download).
  • ILRI Publications â Smallholder Irrigation and Market Access in East Africa (free repository).
  • FAO â Solar-Powered Irrigation Systems: A Clean-Energy, Low-Emission Option for Agriculture (free PDF).

This Practical Reference is intended to be used alongside Lessons 1â5 of the Agricultural Irrigation Technician course. Figures are indicative and must be verified against local supplier pricing, national regulations, and site-specific water tests before quoting or installing.

quiz.q: Which component in a drip irrigation system is primarily responsible for preventing clogging by trapping debris before it reaches the emitters?
options: A) Pressure regulator
B) Filter
C) Backflow preventer
D) Air release valve
quiz.explanation: Filters capture sand, silt, and organic matter before water enters the lateral lines, protecting emitters from clogging.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a pressure regulator in an agricultural irrigation system?
options: A) To increase water pressure for long runs
B) To measure the total water volume used
C) To maintain a consistent downstream pressure
D) To inject fertilizer into the water line
quiz.explanation: A pressure regulator reduces and holds a steady outlet pressure so emitters and sprinklers operate within their designed range.

quiz.q: Which soil moisture sensor type measures water content by detecting the dielectric constant of the soil?
options: A) Tensiometer
B) Gypsum block
C) Granular matrix sensor
D) Capacitance probe
quiz.explanation: Capacitance probes use the soil dielectric constant to estimate volumetric water content, giving fast and repeatable readings.

quiz.q: When performing routine maintenance on a micro-sprinkler system, what is the recommended first step before inspecting emitters?
options: A) Flush the lateral lines to remove accumulated sediment
B) Increase the system pressure to maximum
C) Add chlorine at full strength to every line
D) Replace all emitters regardless of condition
quiz.explanation: Flushing laterals first clears sediment that could otherwise be pushed into emitters during inspection or replacement.

quiz.q: Which factor most directly determines the application rate of a solid-set sprinkler system?
options: A) The color of the sprinkler nozzles
B) The nozzle size and operating pressure
C) The length of the mainline pipe
D) The type of pump fuel used
quiz.explanation: Nozzle diameter and operating pressure together control flow rate and thus the precipitation application rate.

quiz.q: What is the primary function of a chemigation check valve in an irrigation system?
options: A) To filter chemical solutions before injection
B) To prevent irrigation water from flowing back into the chemical supply
C) To measure the pH of the injected solution
D) To increase chemical injection pressure
quiz.explanation: A chemigation check valve stops backflow that could contaminate the water source or chemical tank.

quiz.q: Which method is best for detecting a buried lateral line leak in a subsurface drip irrigation system?
options: A) Visual inspection of the soil surface only
B) Listening with a stethoscope at the pump
C) Monitoring flow meter readings and soil wetness patterns
D) Checking the color of the water at the emitters
quiz.explanation: Comparing flow meter data with expected values and observing unusually wet or dry soil zones helps locate hidden leaks.

quiz.q: What is the correct action if a pressure gauge on a drip system reads significantly higher than the design pressure after the filter?
options: A) Open the flush valve and continue normal operation
B) Add more emitters to the zone
C) Reduce the pump speed without checking the filter
D) Shut down the system and inspect for a clogged filter or closed valve
quiz.explanation: High post-filter pressure usually indicates a blockage or closed valve downstream, so the system should be shut down and inspected.

quiz.q: Which irrigation method is generally most water-efficient for a smallholder vegetable plot in a semi-arid African region?
options: A) Flood irrigation
B) Furrow irrigation
C) Drip irrigation
D) Sprinkler irrigation
quiz.explanation: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the root zone, minimizing evaporation and runoff, making it the most efficient option in water-scarce areas.

quiz.q: A farmer in Kenya draws water from a shallow well 6 m below ground with a suction pump. What is the main limitation of this setup?
options: A) Suction pumps cannot lift water more than about 7 to 8 m
B) Suction pumps require three-phase electricity
C) Suction pumps cannot handle muddy water
D) Suction pumps only work with solar panels
quiz.explanation: Atmospheric pressure limits suction lift to roughly 7 to 8 m at sea level, so deeper wells require submersible or other pump types.

quiz.q: Which water source is most likely to require the heaviest filtration before drip irrigation?
options: A) Deep borehole water
B) Municipal piped water
C) Rainwater from a clean tank
D) River water carrying silt and organic matter
quiz.explanation: Surface water such as rivers carries suspended solids and organics that clog emitters, so it needs the most robust filtration.

quiz.q: A solar-powered pump system is being designed for a farm in Senegal. Which factor most directly determines the daily water volume the system can deliver?
options: A) The colour of the storage tank
B) The peak sun hours and total pump head
C) The length of the suction hose only
D) The number of emitters per plant
quiz.explanation: Daily output depends on available solar energy (peak sun hours) and the total head the pump must overcome, not on tank colour or hose length alone.

quiz.q: In a drip irrigation network, what is the primary purpose of a pressure regulator?
options: A) To increase pump speed
B) To filter sand from water
C) To maintain consistent emitter flow across the block
D) To measure soil moisture
quiz.explanation: Pressure regulators keep pressure within the emitter operating range so all emitters deliver similar flow rates.

quiz.q: Which emitter type is best suited for a field where the farmer wants to adjust the wetted area and flow rate over time?
options: A) Inline pressure-compensating dripper
B) Adjustable micro-sprinkler or variable emitter
C) Soaker hose
D) Punch-in button dripper with fixed flow
quiz.explanation: Adjustable micro-sprinklers allow the farmer to change flow and coverage as crop needs change.

quiz.q: A 1-hectare field needs 5 mm of water per day. How many cubic metres of water are required daily?
options: A) 5 cubic metres
B) 50 cubic metres
C) 500 cubic metres
D) 5000 cubic metres
quiz.explanation: 1 mm over 1 ha equals 10 cubic metres, so 5 mm equals 50 cubic metres per day.

quiz.q: Which soil type has the lowest available water holding capacity and therefore requires more frequent irrigation?
options: A) Clay
B) Silt loam
C) Sandy soil
D) Clay loam
quiz.explanation: Sandy soils have large pores and drain quickly, holding little plant-available water, so they need lighter, more frequent irrigation.

quiz.q: A soil moisture tension of 40 kPa is measured in a tomato field. What does this reading indicate?
options: A) The soil is saturated and irrigation should stop
B) The soil is at field capacity
C) The soil is getting dry and irrigation may be needed
D) The soil is frozen
quiz.explanation: Higher tension means water is held more tightly and is less available to plants; 40 kPa often signals the need to irrigate many vegetables.

quiz.q: Which irrigation scheduling approach uses crop water use estimates based on weather data?
options: A) Feel and appearance method
B) Evapotranspiration replacement method
C) Calendar method only
D) Visual wilting method
quiz.explanation: The ET replacement method estimates crop water use from weather data and replaces that amount through irrigation.

quiz.q: A farmer irrigates every day for 10 minutes regardless of weather. What is the main risk of this practice?
options: A) Over-irrigation during cool or rainy periods and under-irrigation during hot spells
B) It always saves water
C) It eliminates the need for filtration
D) It increases soil salinity automatically
quiz.explanation: Fixed schedules ignore changing crop water demand and rainfall, leading to both over- and under-irrigation.

quiz.q: What is the main function of a sand filter in a drip system using river water?
options: A) Remove dissolved salts
B) Remove large organic and mineral particles
C) Add nutrients to the water
D) Regulate pressure
quiz.explanation: Sand filters trap larger suspended particles before water reaches finer screen or disc filters and emitters.

quiz.q: During maintenance, a technician finds emitters at the end of a drip line have lower flow than those near the inlet. What is the most likely cause?
options: A) Too much filtration
B) Excessive pressure loss along the lateral
C) The pump is too small
D) The soil is too wet
quiz.explanation: Friction loss along the lateral reduces pressure at the far end, lowering emitter flow unless pressure-compensating emitters are used.

quiz.q: Which practice best prevents clogging of drip emitters when using borehole water high in calcium carbonate?
options: A) Increasing pump pressure
B) Periodic acid injection and flushing
C) Adding sand to the water
D) Using larger emitters only
quiz.explanation: Acid injection dissolves mineral scale, and flushing removes loosened deposits, preventing emitter clogging.

quiz.q: A pump delivers 10 cubic metres per hour. How long will it take to apply 30 cubic metres of water?
options: A) 1 hour
B) 2 hours
C) 3 hours
D) 5 hours
quiz.explanation: Time equals volume divided by flow rate: 30 divided by 10 equals 3 hours.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a key advantage of solar-powered irrigation for off-grid farms in Africa?
options: A) It works equally well at night without storage
B) It reduces fuel costs and can be more reliable than diesel pumps
C) It requires no maintenance at all
D) It can pump unlimited water regardless of panel size
quiz.explanation: Solar pumps cut recurring fuel costs and are often more reliable where diesel supply is difficult, though they need maintenance and proper sizing.

quiz.q: In a drip irrigation design, what does the term emission uniformity describe?
options: A) The colour of the dripper
B) How evenly water is applied across the field
C) The speed of the pump
D) The depth of the water table
quiz.explanation: Emission uniformity measures how consistently emitters deliver water throughout the system.

quiz.q: A technician needs to size a pump for a field with a total dynamic head of 25 m and a required flow of 8 cubic metres per hour. Which pump specification is most relevant?
options: A) Pump curve showing 8 cubic metres per hour at 25 m head
B) Pump weight only
C) Pump colour
D) Pump voltage only
quiz.explanation: The pump must be selected using its performance curve to match both the required flow and total dynamic head.

quiz.q: Which business skill is most important for an irrigation technician who wants to grow a service business in a rural area?
options: A) Ignoring customer feedback
B) Accurate quoting, record keeping, and follow-up service
C) Buying the cheapest tools regardless of quality
D) Avoiding training on new technologies
quiz.explanation: Accurate quotes, records, and reliable follow-up build trust and repeat business, which are essential for growth.

quiz.q: A farmer reports that a solar pump runs but delivers no water at midday. Which is the most likely first check?
options: A) The colour of the solar panels
B) Water level in the source and any blockage in the suction or delivery line
C) The brand of the drip tape
D) The soil type in the field
quiz.explanation: If the pump runs but no water moves, low water level, air locks, or blockages are the first practical checks.

quiz.q: What is the recommended action if a screen filter shows a pressure difference greater than the manufacturer limit?
options: A) Ignore it until the end of the season
B) Clean or backwash the filter
C) Increase the pump speed
D) Remove the filter screen
quiz.explanation: A high pressure differential indicates a clogged filter, which must be cleaned or backwashed to protect emitters.

quiz.q: Which combination best represents a complete irrigation scheduling decision?
options: A) When to irrigate and how much to apply
B) Only the pump brand
C) Only the pipe diameter
D) Only the emitter colour
quiz.explanation: Scheduling requires deciding both the timing and the depth of water to apply based on crop, soil, and climate.
